angle: An AI cleanup of 3 years of renewal data showed the renewal rate was worse than the board was told
post_first_line: Three years of renewals, left untouched.
linkedin_post:
Three years of renewals, left untouched.

What the cleanup uncovered changed the conversation in the boardroom.

Jeff Ignacio cleaned up a company's renewal database after the renewal process had been neglected for three years. Renewals from 2023 to 2024 were missing entirely.

So the work started with reconciling the records against Stripe data. Customers were still paying, which made it possible to rebuild the 2025 renewal base from actual payments.

From there, Jeff built out closed-lost opportunities so the team could run win rate analysis on renewals.

The result: the renewal rate was much worse than the company believed. It was also worse than what had been pitched to the board.

Not a happy outcome. But it's the kind of ROI that matters. Once the gap was visible, the response was immediate: customers are churning, all hands on deck, plug the gap.

You can't fix a leak you can't see. Messy data doesn't just slow reporting down. It hides the number that matters most.

When did you last check your renewal data against payments?

Slide 2: Renewals from 2023 to 2024 were missing entirely.
Slide 3: Jeff Ignacio reconciled the records against Stripe payment data.
Slide 4: Customers were still paying, so the 2025 base could be rebuilt.
Slide 5: Closed-lost opportunities were built to enable renewal win rate analysis.
Slide 6: The real renewal rate was much worse than the board was told.
Slide 7: Not a happy outcome, but that's ROI: the gap became visible.
Slide 8: Messy data hides the number that matters most.

lesson.title: Clean renewal data exposes the churn you can't see
takeaways: Neglected renewal tracking can hide a renewal rate far worse than leadership believes.
Payment data like Stripe can serve as the source of truth to rebuild missing renewal records.
Tracking closed-lost renewals lets you run win rate analysis, not just count churn.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last 12 months of payments and compare them to the renewals logged in your CRM. List every customer who is missing or mismatched, then recalculate your renewal rate from that list.

angle: The deals that 'close this month' and never do: how I stopped doing slipped-deal postmortems by hand
post_first_line: Every deal in commit says "closing this month."
linkedin_post:
Every deal in commit says "closing this month."

Most of them never do, and I used to find out the hard way.

Anyone who's worked in RevOps knows this one. A rep says it will close this month, it sits in commit, and then it slips.

Every week we have a leadership call on forecast. I was the one bringing up the slipped deals. Asking the rep "why did this slip?" only gets me so much context.

So I stopped doing the postmortems by hand and built an agent to do them.

It goes through all the calls, reads the notes, and works out what was missing. It looks for the risks the rep actually flagged. Then it checks my calendar for the next forecast leadership meeting.

Before that meeting, it drops a summary into my Slack. The original close date. The root cause. What the rep missed.

I walk into the forecast call with context from the actual conversations instead of a rep's recap after the fact.

The analysis got better because it stopped depending on memory and opinion.

How do you handle slipped deals today?
carousel: Slide 1: Every deal in commit says it closes this month.
Slide 2: Most never do. RevOps finds out at forecast review.
Slide 3: Asking the rep why it slipped gives you thin context.
Slide 4: I built an agent to run the postmortem instead.
Slide 5: It reviews the calls and notes, then flags missing risks.
Slide 6: It checks my calendar for the next forecast meeting.
Slide 7: Before that call, a summary lands in my Slack.
Slide 8: Original close date, root cause, and what the rep missed.

lesson.title: Automate the slipped-deal postmortem
takeaways: Rep recaps after a slip are thin context. The calls and notes hold the real story.
Time the analysis to your forecast meeting so it arrives right when you need it.
A consistent format (original close date, root cause, what the rep missed) makes slips comparable week to week.
lesson.exercise: Pick the last three deals that slipped from commit. For each, write down the original close date, the root cause, and any risk the rep flagged on a call. That's the template to automate.

angle: I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector so you don't have to. Here's the workaround
post_first_line: I vibe coded a Salesforce MCP connector.
linkedin_post:
I vibe coded a Salesforce MCP connector.

I don't recommend you do the same.

I went deep down this rabbit hole because I needed an MCP that could read Salesforce data and give me real analysis. It was a pain.

The build meant writing Apex code and then deploying it. That is a lot of work for something you can route around.

Here's the workaround I'd use instead.

First, find a connector with an MCP that can read a database. CData is one example. That gets you the schema.

Second, use a middleware layer to feed the data in, and run the analysis on the other side.

You get the same outcome without building and maintaining custom Apex.

I learned this the hard way so you can skip it. Vibe coding is fun, but it isn't always the right call for a connector.

What's the last thing you over-engineered?
carousel: Slide 1: I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector.
Slide 2: Please don't repeat my mistake.
Slide 3: It meant building and deploying custom Apex code.
Slide 4: That's a lot of work for one connector.
Slide 5: Start with a connector whose MCP can read a database.
Slide 6: CData is one option. It gives you the schema.
Slide 7: Then use middleware to feed data in for analysis.
Slide 8: Same outcome, no custom Apex to maintain.

lesson.title: Don't build the Salesforce MCP connector yourself
takeaways: Building a custom Salesforce MCP connector means writing and deploying Apex code, which is a lot of overhead.
A connector like CData has an MCP that can read a database, which gives you the schema.
Middleware can feed the data in so you still get the analysis without custom builds.
lesson.exercise: List the data sources your AI workflow needs. For each one, check whether an existing connector or middleware can feed it in before you write any custom code.

angle: Stop writing your own prompts: have Claude rewrite them using your CRM schema
linkedin_post:
Stop writing your own prompts.

I hand that job to Claude, and the way it does it changed how I work.

I have a skill I run with a /prompt-enhancer command. I drop in my rough prompt, which already has a fair amount of context, and Claude goes through my metadata and the Salesforce schema before rewriting it.

I said "new business." Claude worked out that I meant opportunity type: New Business. So it excluded expansions, renewals, and all of that. It also pulled in the right forecast category names.

Then it restructured the prompt into the original ask, the intent, and the action that needs to happen.

We use SPICE internally, and I had notes on it sitting in there. Claude went in and found the applicable fields on its own, including ones I hadn't mentioned. That part was mind-blowing.

The prompt isn't the hard part. The hard part is translating how you talk about the business into how your CRM actually stores it.

Claude already has the schema, so let it do that translation.

What would you hand off to Claude first?
carousel: Slide 1: Stop writing your own prompts for CRM work.
Slide 2: I run a prompt enhancer skill before every query.
Slide 3: Claude reads my metadata and the Salesforce schema first.
Slide 4: I said "new business." It mapped that to opportunity type New Business.
Slide 5: Expansions and renewals got excluded without me asking.
Slide 6: It structured the prompt: original, intent, then action.
Slide 7: It found SPICE-relevant fields I never mentioned.
Slide 8: Let Claude translate your language into your schema.

lesson.title: Let Claude rewrite your prompts using your CRM schema
takeaways: Your shorthand like "new business" rarely matches how the CRM stores the data, and Claude can map one to the other.
A prompt enhancer skill can structure a rough ask into original, intent, and action.
If your methodology notes (like SPICE) are in context, Claude can find the relevant fields you didn't think to name.
lesson.exercise: Create a prompt-enhancer skill that reads your CRM schema, then run one of your rough prompts through it and compare the original with the rewrite.

caption: Let Claude write your prompts

angle: Don't use your smartest model for every step. Scoring 15,000 accounts of sales calls cost about $30
linkedin_post:
$30 to score 15,000 accounts.

The trick is knowing which model not to use.

Jeff Ignacio walked through how to analyze the full history of a sales team's calls. The classification step doesn't need your smartest model. A lower-level model like Claude Haiku works, not Claude Sonnet. If you're bold, something like DeepSeek on a Fireworks API brings costs down even further.

Jeff's estimate for 15,000 accounts: about $30 to analyze the entire history of that sales team.

The cheap run makes room for better questions. Once the data is classified, you can look at what MEDDIC averaged across the team, then build a time series. Did a rep improve over time?

You can compare reps who were regrettable attrition against non-regrettable attrition. Was there a difference between the two? Did improvement in MEDDIC correlate with improvement in performance?

Those are second, third, and fourth order questions. Most teams never get to them because they're still stuck building surface level reporting.

Which step in your workflow is overpaying for a smart model?
carousel: Slide 1: Scoring 15,000 accounts cost about $30.
Slide 2: Don't use your smartest model for every step.
Slide 3: Classification can run on Claude Haiku, not Sonnet.
Slide 4: If you're bold, try DeepSeek on a Fireworks API.
Slide 5: Cheap classification lets you analyze a team's entire history.
Slide 6: Track MEDDIC averages, then build a time series per rep.
Slide 7: Compare regrettable and non-regrettable attrition reps.
Slide 8: Stop at surface reporting and you never ask better questions.

lesson.title: Match the model to the step
takeaways: Classification steps don't need your most powerful model; a lower-level model like Claude Haiku can handle them.
Dropping to a cheaper model cut the estimate to about $30 for 15,000 accounts.
Low cost lets you ask deeper questions like rep improvement over time and attrition differences.
lesson.exercise: List every step in one of your AI workflows. Mark which ones are simple classification, then rerun just those on a cheaper model and compare cost and output.

caption: $30 for 15,000 accounts

angle: Leadership analyses that took a week now take a couple of hours, and that's how RevOps proves AI ROI
post_first_line: One week down to a couple of hours.
linkedin_post:
One week down to a couple of hours.

That's the only AI ROI number my leadership team actually cares about.

The analyses I spin up for leadership used to take me about a week. Now they take a couple of hours.

The result is that leaders make decisions much faster than they used to. That speed is the ROI, and it's visible to the people who sign off on budget.

Then I take it one step further. I have Claude help put a dollar amount on that time and speed gain.

Once you can bring a dollar figure to leadership, you're speaking their language. That's when the ROI stops being a vague claim and starts getting proven.

RevOps doesn't need a fancy AI business case. Pick one recurring analysis, track how long it took before and after, and attach a number to the difference.

How are you proving AI ROI to leadership?

Time saved on a recurring analysis is the simplest before-and-after comparison.
Putting a dollar amount on the gain speaks leadership's language and makes the ROI stick.
